content: A mammogram is an X-ray image of the breast. Physicians utilize mammograms to detect early indications of breast cancer. Routine mammograms can identify breast cancer at an early stage, sometimes up to three years before a lump can be physically felt. To perform a mammogram, you will stand in front of a specialized X-ray machine. A technologist will position your breast on a plastic plate, and another plate will compress your breast from above. This compression flattens the breast and keeps it still while the X-ray is taken. You may experience some pressure during this process. The procedure is repeated to capture a side view of the breast, and the same steps are performed for the other breast. Afterward, you will wait briefly while the technologist ensures the images are clear and do not need to be retaken. It is important to note that the technologist cannot provide you with the results of your mammogram. A radiologist, a physician with specialized training, will review the X-ray images to identify early signs of breast cancer or other abnormalities. Each mammogram may appear slightly different because every woman’s breasts are unique. For most women, undergoing a mammogram is uncomfortable, and some may find it painful. However, the procedure only lasts a few moments, and the discomfort is temporary. The level of discomfort you experience depends on factors such as the technologist’s skill, the size of your breasts, and the degree of compression required. Your breasts may also be more sensitive if you are about to start or are currently on your menstrual period. To prepare for a mammogram, avoid scheduling it during the week before or during your period, as your breasts may be tender or swollen. On the day of the mammogram, refrain from using deodorant, perfume, or powder, as these products can appear as white spots on the X-ray. Some women prefer to wear a two-piece outfit, such as a top with a skirt or pants, so they only need to undress from the waist up for the procedure. If you are concerned about the cost of a mammogram, the CDC provides free or low-cost mammograms through the National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program. You can check if you qualify for this program. You will typically receive the results of your mammogram within a few weeks, although the exact timing depends on the facility. A radiologist will interpret your mammogram and send the results to both you and your doctor. If there is a concern, the mammography facility will contact you sooner. If you do not receive your results within 30 days, reach out to your healthcare provider or the mammography facility. If your mammogram results are normal, continue to have mammograms at the recommended intervals. Comparing current mammograms with previous ones allows radiologists to detect any changes in your breast tissue over time. If your mammogram results are abnormal, it does not necessarily mean you have cancer. Additional mammograms, tests, or examinations will be required to determine the cause of the abnormality. You may be referred to a breast specialist or surgeon for further evaluation. This does not automatically mean you have cancer or require surgery. These specialists are experts in diagnosing breast conditions and will conduct follow-up tests to confirm whether breast cancer is present or to rule it out. If you have questions about mammograms, you can speak with your regular doctor. Alternatively, you can contact the National Cancer Institute for more information. For Medicare-related inquiries, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) or visit the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services website.
